title: harness-bridge policy
description:
What this repository allows, requires and watches. The file lives at .pi/harness-bridge/policy.json and is merged over the bridge's built-in defaults, so every block is optional and an absent block means the default behaviour, not no behaviour. Nothing here is inferred: if the bridge enforces, requires or reports something, that decision is written down, and a decision that is not written down does not happen.

How to write one:
  1. `harness-bridge policy init` writes a full default policy you can edit, and writes policy.schema.json beside it, so an editor with JSON Schema support completes and validates as you type.
  2. `harness-bridge policy check` reports the effective policy after merging, and exits non-zero when a declaration cannot work -- an unknown ledger kind, a metric rule with both or neither threshold.
  3. `harness-bridge policy audit` reports declarations that are valid but do nothing useful: a rule whose pattern matches everyday commands, or one that fights a blocking gate.

Where to put your reasoning: JSON has no comments, and the reason a rule exists is part of the rule. The fields `reason`, `why`, `note`, `message` and `source` are read back by the tools and printed where the decision applies, so a policy that explains itself needs no separate document.

Merging: a repository policy is merged over the defaults block by block. Single values fall back to the default when absent. Lists such as `rules`, `protectedPaths` and `processes.metrics.rules` are replaced wholesale by a layer that declares them, never concatenated: a rule deleted from a policy must stop firing, and a concatenated list would keep it alive invisibly.

$schema.description: Optional. Where the schema for this file is. `policy init` sets it to the copy written beside the policy, so an editor validates the file without a network fetch.

version.description: Policy schema version. Version 1 is the only version the bridge writes, and it is the one required key: reading a file written for another schema silently is how a policy ends up meaning something other than it says.

protectedBranches.description: Branch names that must not be pushed to directly. The check is on the branch a push would update, so a feature branch whose name merely contains `main` is not protected. Leave it empty in a repository with no remote, where protecting the only branch would refuse every commit.

branchNamePattern.description: Regular expression a new branch name must match when `branchNameAction` is not `allow`. It is evaluated against the name being created, not the current branch, so an existing branch that predates the policy is not retroactively invalid.

branchNameAction.description: What an offending branch name means. `warn` reports it and continues, which is the default because a branch name is a convention rather than a hazard. `block` refuses the creation; use it only where a naming scheme is load-bearing for automation.

rules.description: Behavioural rules, evaluated against the thing they describe before an action runs. Each rule names one fact (a command, a path, file content, a commit message, a diff), one pattern to match it, and what a match means. Several rules can match at once: the most restrictive action wins and every matching rule is reported, so a block does not hide the warnings beside it.

examples.reason: Force pushing rewrites shared history; open a new commit instead.

protectedPaths.description: Directories and files whose contents are load-bearing: generated records, contracts, fixtures a run is measured against. A protected path is a statement that a change to it is a change to what the repository means, so the reason is required and is printed with the finding.

examples.reason: The golden fixtures are the ground truth the pipeline is measured against; changing one to make a run pass is the regression this repository exists to catch.

verification.description: The runs that verify this repository, declared rather than reconstructed from CI YAML, a pre-push hook and a README. `verify list` prints them; `verify run` executes them.

lease.description: Who else is writing this tree, from the fleet's lease store (packages/pi-fleet/src/runtime/workspace_lease.ts). Disabled by default.

action.description:
What a finding means. The four levels are ordered and the strictest match wins:
  allow    - recorded and permitted; useful for watching a pattern before deciding what it means.
  warn     - recorded, reported to the reviewer, and the action proceeds.
  escalate - requires a human decision. An unattended caller (a git hook, CI, a headless agent) cannot answer, so `escalation.noApprover` decides: `fail` refuses the action, `warn` turns it into a notice for the reviewer.
  block    - refused, always, in every context. Nothing in the policy can soften a block.

rule.description: One fact about one kind of action, and what it means. A rule is deliberately single-purpose: two facts in one rule cannot be reported, relaxed or tightened separately.

id.description: Stable identifier, quoted in findings and in the audit log. Renaming a rule starts a new history for it, so prefer a new rule over a renamed one.

scope.description: A grouping label for humans and for `policy check` summaries, for example `destructive-git` or `frozen-artifacts`. It carries no enforcement: it is how a reader finds the rules that belong together.

tool.description: Which tool the rule applies to: `bash`, `write`, `edit`, `read`, or `*` for any. A rule for bash looks at the command; a rule for write or edit looks at the path and, for content rules, at the text.

kind.description:
What the pattern is matched against:
  command        - a shell command line, as bash will receive it.
  path           - the path an action would write or read.
  content        - text being written, matched line by line.
  commit-message - the message of a commit being created.
  diff           - the staged or proposed diff as text.

pattern.description: Regular expression source, in the syntax the runtime provides. It is searched rather than anchored, so anchor it yourself where that matters. A pattern that matches everyday work is the most common policy mistake, and it is what `policy audit` exists to find: a rule matching too much is indistinguishable from a policy that blocks everything.

flags.description: Regular expression flags for `pattern`, as the regex engine spells them, e.g. `i` for case-insensitive. Case-insensitivity is the common case and the reason this is not folded into the pattern: `--force` and `--FORCE` are the same hazard, and a pattern carrying its own inline flags is harder to read at a glance.

reason.description: Why this rule exists, in the words of the people who will hit it. Printed with the finding, so a refused action explains itself without a trip to a document.

source.description: Where the rule comes from: a standard, an incident, an ADR, a checklist item. Lets a reviewer check the rule against its origin instead of guessing.

glob.description: Path glob, matched against repository-relative paths. `**` crosses directories; `*` does not.

action.description: What a change to a protected path means. `warn` is the common choice: the change is often right, and it needs a human to say so.

reason.description: What makes this path load-bearing. Required, because a frozen path without a reason gets ignored the first time it is inconvenient.

source.description: Where the protection comes from, for a reviewer who wants to check whether it still applies.

protectedPath.description: One entry in protectedPaths: a glob whose contents are load-bearing, and what a change to them means. The reason is required because the check is a claim about the repository's meaning rather than a preference, and a reader who disagrees with it needs something to disagree with.

processes.description:
Declared processes: a named discipline with stages and gates. SDLC is one, and the shape is general by design -- a research pipeline, a document workflow or a release train is the same thing with different gates.

The concepts, in the order they matter:
  process     - a discipline whose steps must leave evidence. It has stages (where work happens) and gates (what must be true at a boundary).
  gate        - a requirement that certain evidence exists before an action proceeds, plus the consequence when it does not. It is not a checklist item: it names the tools, paths, commands or reads that count as evidence, so `the tests were run` is checked rather than assumed.
  enforcement - what happens without the evidence: `block` refuses the action, `nudge` reports it and allows the action so the record shows the miss, `off` disables the gate.
  firing      - evidence for a gate was observed. A miss is a gated action attempted without it. The ledger records both, which is what the metrics block counts.
  park        - a boundary waiting for a person. Parking is deliberate and is never counted as a miss: the workflow is doing what it was told to do.

Gates are enforced while work happens; the ledger of firings, misses and parked boundaries is what `process report`, `process metrics` and the improvement loop read afterwards. A policy that declares gates but no metrics still enforces them; a policy that declares metrics has said what to watch for over time.

enabled.description: Process ids that are active. Empty means every known definition is active. A process declared under `definitions` is active whether or not it is listed here, unless it is switched off in `disabled`: declaring a process is itself a statement that it applies.

definitions.description: Processes by id. An entry either tightens a built-in process, naming only what changes, or defines a new one, naming everything.

disabled.description: Gates switched off, as `processId/gateId` or a bare gate id when it is unambiguous across processes. A disabled gate is dropped before evaluation and leaves no record, which is why a reader cannot tell it from a gate that is no longer declared: use `waivers` when the decision itself is the point.

waivers.description: Built-in gates this repository has exempted, each with the reason it does not apply and the command that shows it. A waived gate stays active and the guard reports it as waived instead of missing, so the ledger holds the decision rather than an absence. A waiver outranks `disabled` for the same gate, because the recorded reason is the whole point.

examples.reason: this repository produces presentations with a different linter, so the shipped deck linter does not exist here

processOverride.description: A process, either defined whole or tightened field by field over a built-in one.

description.description: What the process covers and what it deliberately leaves out.

source.description: Where the process comes from: a convention, a standard, an ADR. A gate that traces to nothing is a gate nobody can argue with.

stages.description: Ordered stage names, e.g. ["plan", "implement", "verify", "ship"]. Gates attach to a stage, which is what orders them and what makes `requiredBefore` meaningful.

gates.description: The gates. Overriding a built-in gate names its id and only the fields that change; declaring a gate id that does not exist adds it.

examples.title: The test suite ran against the current tree
examples.why: A change that ships without its tests leaves the next reader unable to tell intent from accident.

gate.description: One boundary requirement. A gate answers two separate questions and the schema keeps them separate: what counts as evidence (`evidence`), and what happens without it (`enforcement`).

id.description: Gate id, unique within the process and quoted in the ledger, e.g. `no-verify` or `tests-run`.

title.description: Short name shown in reports and in a nudge.

stage.description: Which process stage the gate belongs to. The stage orders gates relative to each other and to the work.

requiredBefore.description: Actions that must not proceed before this gate has fired. Matching is by substring against the action, for example `git push`, so a gate can be required before a command an agent chooses freely.

why.description: What goes wrong without the gate. Printed when the gate fires against an action, which is the moment the reason is worth reading.

source.description: Where the requirement comes from, so it can be checked rather than obeyed.

evidenceTtlMinutes.description: How long a firing counts as current, in minutes. A gate satisfied by an hour-old test run is satisfied by a test run that predates the change under discussion. Absent or non-positive means the evidence never expires, which is the historical behaviour and the right choice for gates about things that do not change, such as reading a specification.

gateEvidence.description: What counts as satisfying the gate. Each list is a set of alternatives and the gate fires when one of them is observed. An empty list means that route cannot satisfy the gate, which is different from a gate with no routes at all: the second can never fire, and `policy audit` says so.

tools.description: Tool names whose use can satisfy the gate, e.g. ["bash"] or ["write", "edit"]. Use it for gates about doing something rather than about a specific command.

paths.description: Globs of files whose creation or modification counts as evidence: an artifact the gate is really about.

commands.description: Regular expressions matched against a command that ran. This is the strongest local evidence available: it says how the fact was established, not merely that something was.

reads.description: Paths that count as evidence when read, for gates that require reading a document before acting on it.

enforcement.description:
What happens when the gate is not satisfied:
  block - the action is refused. Use it where proceeding is unrecoverable or leaves no record.
  nudge - the action proceeds and the miss is recorded, so the discipline is visible without stopping work. The improvement loop reads those misses and can propose tightening the gate.
  off   - the gate does not fire, and that is recorded like a disabled gate.

processSettings.description: Per-process knobs that are not gates: how much leniency the improvement loop allows, and what this repository treats as the process's own gate command.

nudgeTolerance.description: How many observed misses a nudge tolerates before the loop proposes promoting the gate to a block. A low tolerance means the proposal arrives early, which is right where misses are rare; raising it states that the misses are acceptable for now.

gateCommands.description: Commands this repository treats as running the process's gates, for example a make target that runs lint, tests and the ladder. Naming them makes a project-specific entry point first-class instead of teaching every agent a different command.

options.description: Process-specific settings, free-form by design and read by the process that understands them. Keeping them here rather than inventing schema for each is what lets a new process exist without a bridge release.

gateWaiver.description: One exemption from a gate the guard would otherwise demand. It exists because the gates ship built in: a repository can be governed by a process convention that describes another repository's work, and the honest answer is a recorded, reviewable exemption rather than a gate silently switched off. The reason and the evidence command are both required, and `process waive` refuses to write one without them.

gate.description: The gate exempted, as `processId/gateId` or a bare gate id when it is unambiguous across processes, e.g. `deck/D2`.

reason.description: Why this gate does not apply here. Required, because an exemption nobody explained cannot be argued with at review time.

evidence.description: The command that shows the gate does not apply: it finds nothing, or fails. Required, so the claim behind the waiver can be re-run instead of believed.

metrics.description:
What to count in the ledger afterwards, and what a count means. Enforcement happens while work happens; this block is the other half of the same discipline -- the thresholds this team considers a problem. They belong in the policy because the bridge cannot know them. Whether a boundary parked twice in a week is diligence or a bottleneck, whether a gate that never missed is habitual or untested: those are judgements about a workflow, and a hard-coded threshold would be one team's opinion wearing a tool's clothes.

Rules are reported, never enforced. A fired rule is printed by `process metrics` and `process report` and gives a non-zero exit code; acting on a metric stays a decision the improvement loop proposes rather than one it takes.

observationKinds.description: Which ledger events count as reaching a gate at all. This is the denominator of the miss rate, and it is why `gate-parked` is absent by default: being held at a boundary is the gate doing its job, and counting it as an observation would reward waiting with a lower miss rate. Include it when, in this repository, reaching a human boundary is the interesting event.

rules.description: Count-based rules over the ledger. No rules by default: the bridge does not decide what a team should worry about.

examples.message: a boundary was parked twice this week: either the approver is the bottleneck or the question is not answerable as asked
no gated action in 30 days: either the pipeline is unused or its gates are not being evaluated, and the second is the one worth knowing

metricRule.description: A count of ledger events with a scope and a threshold. Exactly one of `atLeast` and `atMost` is required: they are two different questions -- `this happens more than it should` and `this is not happening at all` -- and a rule declaring both would be unreadable rather than stricter.

id.description: Identifier quoted in the finding, so a firing points at the declaration that produced it.

kinds.description: Which ledger events the rule counts. Absent means every event, which is how a question about liveness is asked: has anything happened at all.

gateId.description: Count only events naming this gate, e.g. `tests-run`. Use it to watch one boundary rather than a whole process.

processId.description: Count only events naming this process, e.g. `sdlc`. Use it where several processes share one ledger.

windowDays.description: Rolling window in days, counted back from when the rule is evaluated. Absent means the whole ledger, which is right for cumulative questions and wrong for `lately`: a rule about the current state of a workflow usually wants a window.

atLeast.description: Fire when the count is at least this. The threshold for `too much`: misses, parks, nudges ignored.

atMost.description: Fire when the count is at most this, zero included. The threshold for `not happening`: a gate that has never fired, a boundary nobody reached. Absence of evidence is a finding, and this is how a policy says so.

message.description: What the count means, in the team's words. Printed as the finding's text, because the number without the interpretation is the part nobody reads.

metricSeverity.description:
How much attention a fired rule deserves. The severities order the findings so the first line of a report is the one that matters:
  critical - the workflow is not doing what it claims.
  major    - a person needs to look at this week.
  minor    - worth knowing, no action expected.
  note     - context for whoever reads the report.

ledgerKind.description:
The event kinds the ledger records. A rule naming a kind the bridge never writes would look right to its author and never fire, so validation rejects it rather than letting it read as a healthy system:
  gate-fired   - evidence for a gate was observed.
  gate-missing - a gated action was attempted without its evidence.
  gate-parked  - a boundary is waiting for a person's decision.
  nudge        - a miss was reported without refusing the action.
  compliance   - an action was recorded as complying after a nudge.
  promotion    - the improvement loop changed a gate's enforcement.
  rollback     - a promotion was reverted.

ci.description: Where verification runs. The split is deliberate: the local runner is for the loop a person is already in, fast feedback before a push, and the GitHub subset is for the environment nobody controls. Both run the same stage definitions, so a stage cannot quietly mean two things.

local.description: The local runner and the stages it runs.

runner.description: `act` runs the GitHub workflow locally; `direct` runs the stage commands in this checkout. The stages are the same either way: the difference is fidelity against speed, and the runner reports which one it used.

actMode.description: `host` uses an act binary; `container` runs the act image with the docker socket mounted, which is how a machine with only Docker still runs the workflow. The runner picks what is available and says so.

actImage.description: The act image used in container mode.

stages.description: Stage ids run locally, in order. Naming them explicitly is how a repository decides that the slow check is worth its runtime locally, or only in CI.

requireBeforePush.description: Whether a push is refused until the local set passes. The generated runner enforces it, so the setting holds whether the check is run by hand or by the git hook.

image.description: The container image the workflow's job runs in.

platform.description: The platform act should emulate, e.g. linux/amd64.

secretsFile.description: File act reads secrets from, e.g. .act.secrets. It is gitignored by the installer: a secrets file committed to the repository is a leak waiting for its first push.

actTtlMinutes.description: How long an act container may exist before it is reaped. act has no daemon, so this is a TTL on the debris of interrupted runs rather than on a service; it is enforced before and after every invocation.

github.description: The subset that runs in the repository's own CI.

stages.description: Stage ids the workflow runs, usually a subset: the long stages that do not change the answer on every push.

workflow.description: Path of the workflow that carries this subset.

stages.description: Stage definitions by id, shared by both runners. A stage is a command with a reason, which is what makes `ci plan` readable.

unit.title: Unit tests
unit.reason: Fast feedback on the module under change.

ladder.title: Verification ladder
ladder.reason: The complete check; slow, so not on every push.

ciStage.description: One stage. A stage reports three outcomes, not two, and the distinction is what keeps the runner trustworthy: exit 0 means it ran and passed; exit 77 means it does not apply in this environment (the automake convention -- a fixture this repository does not carry, a tool that is not installed); any other non-zero exit means it failed and stops the run. Without the middle case, every machine missing one tool looks broken and people stop reading the runner.

id.description: Stage id, referenced by the local and GitHub stage lists.

title.description: Human-readable name printed by the runner.

command.description: Shell command run from the repository root. It is a plain command line: a stage that needs quoting belongs in a script of its own, referenced by a single word.

long.description: Marks a stage as a poor fit for every push. Long stages run in the full local set and in the pre-push hook only when the fast set is skipped, which keeps the fast path fast without deleting the slow check.

reason.description: Why the stage exists. Quoted in plans and reports so a reader can decide whether it is still worth its runtime.

timeoutSeconds.description: Wall-clock budget in seconds. The runner wraps the stage in timeout; a stage that exceeds it fails.

critical.description: Whether a failure gates the run. Default true; a stage marked false is advisory: reported and counted, and the verdict does not change.

tokenBudget.description: Declared budget for the agent work this stage fronts. Carried and surfaced, not metered by the harness.

unicode.description: Which non-ASCII characters are content and which are a violation. The distinction is the point: mathematical notation, non-Latin scripts and emoji are text, while typographic substitutions (a curly quote where code expects an apostrophe) and invisible characters (a zero-width space inside an identifier) are defects that look like nothing. A policy here states what this repository's files are supposed to be.

enabled.description: Whether the scan runs at all. Disabling it shows in the effective policy that `policy check` prints, so it is a visible decision rather than a silent one.

defaultMode.description: The mode applied to files no scope matches. A strict default loosened per scope is safer than the reverse: the files nobody thought about are usually the machine-read ones.

scopes.description: Per-glob modes, evaluated in order with the first match winning, each carrying the reason it is exempt.

examples.reason: Lean 4 notation is the language's syntax.

ignore.description: Paths the scan does not read, each with its reason. Skipped files are reported with the count, so an exemption is visible rather than a hole.

respectGitignore.description: Also skip whatever git ignores: scratch output that is not part of the repository. A gitignored directory can hold a worktree, which is why `worktrees` is a separate decision.

worktrees.description: `current` scans the checkout the scan started from and names every other worktree it left out, with its branch and whether that branch is merged; `all` scans them too, overruling the ignore rule that hides them. The default is `current` because the other worktree is usually someone else's unfinished work, and the report says which it was.

bannedCharacters.description: Code points that are never allowed, whatever the mode, written as integers rather than as characters so the policy file cannot itself smuggle the character it bans.

bannedRanges.description: Inclusive code point ranges to reject, for classes of characters such as format controls or private use, rather than one entry per character.

allowedRanges.description: Inclusive ranges to accept even where the mode would reject them: this repository's mathematical symbols, or the script its documents are written in.

maxNonAsciiRatio.description: Share of non-ASCII characters a file may contain before it is reported, for files long enough for a ratio to mean something. Catches a file that is mostly not text.

minCodePointsForRatio.description: File length, in code points, below which the ratio is not applied: on a five-character file a single symbol is twenty percent and means nothing.

maxNonAsciiPerLine.description: Non-ASCII characters allowed on one line. Catches what a ratio cannot: one line of a five-thousand-line source file that is a pasted block of typographic quotes.

unicodeMode.description:
How strict the scan is in a scope:
  ascii            - non-ASCII is a finding; for machine-read files and code.
  typographic-free - typographic substitutions and invisible characters are findings while scripts, mathematics and emoji are content; for prose that must stay greppable.
  unrestricted     - recorded but not reported; for files whose text is not this repository's to normalise.

unicodeScope.description: A glob and the strictness that applies to it, with the reason it is exempt.

reason.description: Why this scope differs from the default. A scope without a reason becomes folklore; `policy check` prints it so it can be argued with.

ignoreEntry.description: A path the scan does not read, and why.

reason.description: Why skipping it is safe. Reported with the count of skipped files.

codePointRange.description: An inclusive range of Unicode code points.

resumeBrief.description: Resume-brief injection: whether the recovered-session brief reaches the conversation, from which sources, how often, and whether a reconciliation marker is required so a stale continuation loses its authority in review. Defaults: enabled, the standard brief path, static refresh, optional marker.

enabled.description: Whether the brief is injected at all. False leaves the file on disk untouched; only the injection stops.

sources.description: Candidate brief paths relative to the workspace; the first existing one is used.

refreshMode.description: static injects once per brief revision; annotate adds the reconcile-marker status to every injected copy; refresh re-injects on every call regardless of the signature.

markerPolicy.description: required states the reconcile-marker status on every injected copy and calls out a brief without a marker; optional reports it only in annotate mode.

injection.description: Prompt-injection detection over text this repository does not control: fetched pages, issue bodies, tool output, and agent output that another agent will read. The floor is fixed on purpose -- a handful of detectors cannot be switched off or made weaker, because `obvious injection is allowed here` is not a preference a policy file should be able to express.

enabled.description: Whether detection runs. Disabling it leaves the mandatory detectors in place; the floor is not configurable.

detectors.description: Per-detector overrides by id, each naming only the fields that change (severity, action, title, why). Detectors not named keep their defaults.

disabled.description: Detector ids to switch off. Mandatory detectors are refused here rather than silently kept on, so the policy says what will actually happen.

maxScanChars.description: Text beyond this length is scanned in the head and tail only, and says so. The limit is reported rather than silent: a scan that quietly skipped the middle of a document is worse than no scan.

decodeEncodedPayloads.description: Decode base64 and hex runs and inspect the result, which is how an instruction hidden in an encoded blob is caught. On by default; it costs a second pass over the text.

allowlist.description: Terms this repository has decided are legitimate despite a detector: a security document quoting an attack, a fixture containing the pattern on purpose. Allowlisting one term is narrower than disabling a detector.

escalation.description: What an escalation means when no human can answer it: a git hook, a CI job, an agent acting without a UI. Escalation is the level that asks someone; the question here is what to do when nobody is there to ask.

noApprover.description: `fail`, the default, refuses the action: an escalation that cannot be answered is not an approval. `warn` reports the finding and continues, which suits a repository where the change set is itself under human review and the finding is a notice to that reviewer. Blocks are unaffected either way: credentials, the frozen verification ladder and destructive commands always fail.

note.description: Why this repository chose that. Printed by `policy check`, so the reviewer who wonders why a finding did not stop the run has the answer in front of them.

secrets.description: Credential scanning of content that is about to be committed. The interesting part is not the scanning but the fixture story: a scanner's own test suite has to contain token-shaped strings, and a policy that blocks them pushes people to turn the check off, which is worse than a notice.

action.description: What a finding in ordinary content means. `block` is the usual choice: a real credential in a commit is not recoverable by editing the commit.

allowlist.description: Strings that are not secrets despite matching a pattern: documentation placeholders, example tokens. A narrow allowlist beats relaxing a pattern.

minLength.description: Shortest string considered a candidate. Lowering it finds more and costs precision, which is why the fixture settings matter more than this one.

fixtureGlobs.description: Paths where fake credentials are expected: test fixtures, scanner tests, testdata. A scanner tested only against real-shaped secrets is a scanner nobody has tested.

fixtureAction.description: What a finding inside a fixture path means. `warn` keeps it visible to a reviewer while letting the test suite carry the token-shaped strings it needs.

fixturePatterns.description: Pattern ids to downgrade inside fixture paths; `*` means every pattern. Narrowing this is how a repository keeps blocking a real key that happens to sit under a fixture directory.

capability.description: Capability-scope enforcement for delegated work: when an agent or a pipeline stage runs with a token, this decides whether the scope on that token is checked before an action. A scope nobody verifies is documentation.

mode.description: `block` refuses an action outside the token's scope; `warn` reports it and continues, which is how a repository starts before it trusts the scope table it wrote.

cli.description: The verifier command: the program that inspects a scope and answers allow or refuse. Naming it explicitly lets a repository use its own implementation instead of the bridge's.

timeoutMs.description: How long the verifier may take before the check is treated as failed. Optional; absent keeps the default of 15000 ms. A check that cannot answer inside its budget is not an approval, so the timeout fails closed.

commits.description: Commit-message conventions checked locally, where the message is still cheap to change.

conventional.description: Whether the message must follow the Conventional Commits shape, `type(scope): subject`. Checked before the commit rather than in review, because a message is rewritten in seconds beforehand and by nobody afterwards.

maxSubject.description: Maximum subject length in characters. A limit is a writing constraint: it forces the subject to say one thing.

forbidNoVerify.description: Whether `git commit --no-verify` is refused. The flag exists for emergencies; allowing it by policy means every bypass is deliberate.

audit.description: The record of what the bridge decided: append-only JSON Lines, one entry per decision, and the reason a finding is checkable later by someone who was not there.

path.description: Where the log lives, relative to the repository root.

chain.description: Whether each entry carries a hash of the previous one. A chain does not prevent editing; it makes editing detectable, which is the property that turns a log into evidence. `audit verify` checks it.

recordAllows.description: Whether permitted actions are recorded as well as findings. Recording allows makes the log a complete account of what happened rather than a list of problems, at the cost of volume.

protectedPaths.reason: Fixtures are the ground truth these tests are measured against.

rules.message: a boundary was parked twice this week: either the approver is the bottleneck or the question is not answerable as asked
no gated action in 30 days: either the pipeline is unused or its gates are not being evaluated

escalation.note: An escalation nobody can answer is not an approval.

$comment: The enum lists are stamped from the code by scripts/build_policy_schema.mjs, and test/policy_schema.test.ts holds the schema to the code: the enums are compared against LEDGER_KINDS, METRIC_SEVERITIES and the RuleAction union, every property must carry a description, the top-level keys must match the default policy's, and the metrics constraints are checked against validateMetricsPolicy on the same probe documents.
